passages.original: et utique non posset haec duo, sed actum est, ut haberet auctoritatem imitandum uerum adulterium lenocinante falso tonitru. quis autem paenulatorum magistrorum audit aure sobria ex eodem puluere hominem clamantem et dicentem: fingebat haec Homerus et humana ad deos transferebat; diuina mallem ad nos? sed uerius dicitur, quod fingebat haec quidem ille, sed hominibus flagitiosis diuina tribuendo, ne flagitia flagitia putarentur et ut quisquis ea fecisset, non homines perditos, sed caelestes deos uideretur imitatus.
passages.english: And of course he could not have done these two things, but it was contrived so that real adultery should have authority for imitation, with false thunder acting as its pander. Yet which of the gowned schoolmasters listens with a sober ear to a man from their own dust crying out and saying: "Homer invented these things and transferred human qualities to the gods; I would rather he had transferred divine ones to us"? But it is more truly said that he did indeed invent these things, but by attributing divine qualities to wicked men, so that crimes should not be thought crimes, and so that whoever committed them should seem to have imitated not abandoned men but the gods of heaven.
passages.notes: 'ex eodem puluere' (from the same dust) is taken as 'one of their own trade', i.e. a fellow teacher of literature. The quoted saying is Cicero's (Tusculan Disputations 1.26.65).

passages.original: sed tamen uidetur mihi, domine deus meus — et ita est in conspectu tuo de hac re cor meum — non facile fortasse de hac amputanda consuetudine matrem meam fuisse cessuram, si ab alio prohiberetur, quem non sicut Ambrosium diligebat. quem propter salutem meam maxime diligebat, eam uero ille propter eius religiosissimam conuersationem, qua in bonis operibus tam feruens spiritu frequentabat ecclesiam, ita ut saepe erumperet, cum me uideret, in eius praedicationem gratulans mihi, quod talem matrem haberem, nesciens, qualem illa filium, qui dubitabam de illis omnibus et inueniri posse uiam uitae minime putabam.
passages.english: But yet it seems to me, O Lord my God, and so my heart stands on this matter in your sight, that my mother would perhaps not easily have given way about cutting off this custom had she been forbidden by someone else whom she did not love as she loved Ambrose. She loved him most of all for the sake of my salvation, and he loved her for her most devout way of life, in which, so fervent in spirit in good works, she frequented the church. So he would often break out, when he saw me, into praise of her, congratulating me on having such a mother, not knowing what kind of son she had: one who doubted all those things and did not at all think that the way of life could be found.

passages.original: Gaudebam etiam, quod uetera scripta legis et prophetarum iam non illo oculo mihi legenda proponerentur, quo antea uidebantur absurda, cum arguebam tamquam ita sentientes sanc-. tos tuos; uerum autem non ita sentiebant. et tamquam regulam diligentissime conmendaret, saepe in popularibus sermonibus suis dicentem Ambrosium laetus audiebam: litter.a occidit, spiritus autem uiuificat, cum ea, quae ad litteram peruersitatem docere uidebantur, remoto mystico uelamento spiritaliter aperiret, non dicens quod me offenderet, quamuis ea diceret, quae utrum uera essent adhuc ignorarem.
passages.english: I was glad also that the old writings of the law and the prophets were now set before me to be read not with that eye with which they had previously seemed absurd, when I used to criticise your saints as though they held such views; but in truth they did not hold them. And I used to listen gladly to Ambrose saying often in his sermons to the people, as though he were most carefully commending it as a rule: "The letter kills, but the spirit gives life", while he laid open spiritually, removing the mystical veil, those things which taken literally seemed to teach perversity. He said nothing that offended me, although he said things of which I still did not know whether they were true.
passages.notes: Scanning errors 'sanc-. tos' and 'litter.a' read as 'sanctos' and 'littera'. The quotation is 2 Corinthians 3:6.
